title: CVE-2026-67548 - taOS: Non-Admin Users Can Access System Settings and Update Actions
text:
8.3

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-67548
taOS: Non-Admin Users Can Access System Settings and Update Actions

taOS is a self-hosted AI agent OS. Prior to version 1.0.0-beta.25, tinyagentos (taOS) registers all system settings routes under a single APIRouter() instance created with no admin authorization dependency. Any authenticated user—including non-admin invited users whose is_admin flag is explicitly False—can read the full system configuration, overwrite it, modify platform settings, trigger a git pull + dependency reinstall + service restart, and switch the tracked update branch. Successful exploitation of the write endpoints causes immediate configuration corruption or a denial of service for all users on the instance from a low-privileged account. This issue has been patched in version 1.0.0-beta.25.

title: CVE-2026-67547 - taOS: Authenticated Non-Admin Host Code Execution via Skill Runtime

8.8

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-67547
taOS: Authenticated Non-Admin Host Code Execution via Skill Runtime

taOS is a self-hosted AI agent OS. Prior to version 1.0.0-beta.23, the POST /api/skill-exec/{skill_id}/call endpoint in taOS executes built-in skills — including the code_exec skill which runs arbitrary Python via subprocess.run(["python3", "-c", code]) — without performing any admin role check, skill ownership check, or agent assignment verification. Any authenticated non-admin user can supply attacker-controlled Python code in the request body and have it executed as the taOS backend process user on the host, achieving full remote code execution with no privilege escalation required beyond a valid (non-admin) session. This issue has been patched in version 1.0.0-beta.23.

title: CVE-2026-67546 - Heym: Command execution via POST /api/mcp/fetch-tools stdio transport: supplied command is spawned before MCP validation
text:
8.8

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-67546
Heym: Command execution via POST /api/mcp/fetch-tools stdio transport: supplied command is spawned before MCP validation

Heym builds and runs agentic systems and business-process automations on self-hosted infrastructure. Prior to version 0.0.75, the same POST /api/mcp/fetch-tools endpoint (any authenticated user, lowest role) also accepts the stdio transport, which spawns the attacker-supplied command with attacker-supplied args and an environment merged over os.environ. The process executes on the shared backend host before MCP protocol validation fails — so side effects fire regardless of whether the command speaks MCP. This is a distinct weakness class and exploit primitive from the SSRF (Advisory 2) on the same endpoint, and needs a different fix (role gating / opt-in trust boundary rather than egress controls). This issue has been patched in version 0.0.75.

Heym: Playwright Custom Code Backend RCE via `playwrightCode` Field

Heym builds and runs agentic systems and business-process automations on self-hosted infrastructure. Prior to version 0.0.71, Heym's workflow engine accepts an arbitrary Python code string in the playwrightCode field of a Playwright node. title: CVE-2026-67543 - Heym Unsandboxed skill code execution: skills run via a local backend subprocess without the Docker isolation that Python tools mandate
text:
8.8

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-67543
Heym Unsandboxed skill code execution: skills run via a local backend subprocess without the Docker isolation that Python tools mandate

Heym builds and runs agentic systems and business-process automations on self-hosted infrastructure. Prior to version 0.0.70, heym hardens one untrusted-code path but not its sibling. The Python tool executor (python_tool_executor.py) treats user code as untrusted and mandates a Docker sandbox (no network, read-only fs, non-root, no docker socket), failing closed. The skill executor (skill_python_executor.py) runs skill Python via a local backend subprocess with no Docker isolation — only a 512 MB RLIMIT and a 7-key env denylist — so a skill executes inside the backend execution context, with filesystem access, network egress, and non-denylisted environment variables that should not be exposed to untrusted/shared skills. In the shipped Docker config (backend runs as root + /var/run/docker.sock mounted), this escalates to host root. This issue has been patched in version 0.0.70.

title: CVE-2026-67541 - Heym: Missing role gate in team-member management lets any member add/remove members, exposing team-shared credentials
text:
8.1

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-67541
Heym: Missing role gate in team-member management lets any member add/remove members, exposing team-shared credentials

Heym builds and runs agentic systems and business-process automations on self-hosted infrastructure. Prior to version 0.0.70, team-member management (add / remove / update) is gated only on team membership, not on the team creator/admin role — and TeamMember has no role column. Any non-creator member can seat an attacker account into the team; because credential team-shares are scoped only by TeamMember.user_id, the newly-added attacker can then decrypt every credential shared into that team (provider API keys, OAuth tokens. This issue has been patched in version 0.0.70.

title: N-able Takes N-central Platform Offline After Discovery of 33 Flaws
text: Elizabeth Montalbano,Contributing WriterNovember 11, 20265 Min ReadSource: Panther Media via Alamy Stock Photo N-able is navigating a hectic crisis-management situation after the discovery of more than 30 alleged zero-day flaws in its N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform, as well as the disclosure of exploits allowing attackers to execute commands, create administrator accounts, and escalate privileges to root.Realizing the critical security nature of the situation, N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline earlier this week across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific after offensive security researcher Sean Bales on Sunday publicly revealed the flaws, collectively called Able2Shell, and subsequently published a series of exploits for them on the GitHub account "Oracle-Security." N-able also advised customers operating on-premises servers to shut them down until further notice."N-able sincerely appreciates the patience, flexibility, and partnership our customers have demonstrated throughout this critical security event," the company wrote in a security update Wednesday. The extraordinary scenario has major repercussions for the entire endpoint management industry, including managed service providers (MSPs) and IT managers that broadly use N-central to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely. The risk for users of vulnerable platforms is significant because of the "extraordinary privileges" these RMM platforms have "because they need them to do their jobs," observes Gene Moody, field chief technology officer (CTO) for autonomous endpoint management provider Action 1.N-able and other RMM platforms can engage in critical tasks such as script execution, software deployment, and remote administration, often across many thousands of endpoints, Moody says. The downside? "That also makes them incredibly attractive targets," he says.Indeed, with public exploit code available, attackers already are scanning for vulnerable systems, although no exploitation has yet been observed, N-able reported in a security update Wednesday. The company moved fast to remedy some of the most critical flaws, releasing N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) on Tuesday to address seven CVEs associated with them; the company says it also plans to release further security updates. Multiple Zero-Day Security Bugs in N-ableFlaws covered by the N-able hotfix are tracked as the following: CVE-2026-125883, which covers multiple XXE vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125878, which covers multiple OGNL Injection vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125879, a local privilege escalation flaw; CVE-2026-125880, described as stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata; and CVE-2026-125881, a schema validation flaw. The patch also addresses CVE-2026-125882, which enables remote code execution (RCE) via file repository upload path traversal and was discovered by Nate Fair of Sprocket Security; and CVE-2026-91000, which leads to local privilege escalation via insecure IPC Channels.Though Bales disclosed 33 separate flaws, some of them are steps in longer exploit chains built from other entries on the same list, according to a report from Tenable's Research Special Operations published today. All in all, Bales listed four exploit chains, with the XXE chain emerging as potentially the most significant of the issues, according to Tenable."The researcher describes the XXE chain as credential-free, and N-able's record for CVE-2026-125883 lists no privileges and no user interaction as required," the Tenable team wrote. That chain exploits an unauthenticated XXE flaw in N-central's service-import functionality and can ultimately turn an unauthenticated network request into a complete compromise of a central IT management system.Indeed, the CyberSec Guru called the credential-free XXE exploit the "centerpiece of the release" and went into detail about how it can be exploited to create an attacker entry point into a system in a blog post […]

In November 2023 CACTUS ransomware campaign, threat actors were observed exploiting the flaws to establish a foothold and download additional payloads to establish persistence and remote control by deploying ManageEngine Unified Endpoint Management and Security (UEMS), AnyDesk, and Plink.

Microsoft on Tuesday released patches for a total of 1,259 vulnerabilities spanning its software portfolio, the second consecutive month where the patch volume has exceeded 1,000 flaws.

These cover 726 flaws in Windows, 174 in Office, 61 in Developer Tools, 59 in SQL Server, 53 in Developer Tools, and 27 in SharePoint Server. The patches also include 165 non-Microsoft-issued CVE identifiers. More than 500 flaws relate to elevation of privilege, followed by remote code execution and information disclosure bugs.

With the latest round of fixes, Microsoft has addressed over 5,100 CVEs this year alone, according to Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable.

Of these, a Moderate-severity security flaw in Microsoft Outlook (CVE-2026-124194, CVSS score: 6.5) has been flagged as actively exploited by Microsoft.

"Product UI does not warn users of unsafe actions in Microsoft Office Outlook allows an unauthorized attacker to perform spoofing over a network," Microsoft said in an advisory.

An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and persuade a target to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook.

This, in turn, could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information, such as an NTLMv2 hash, that could be used to impersonate the user.

Microsoft emphasized that successful exploitation requires network connectivity and user interaction. The tech giant credited a researcher named Nono and Anthropic's Benoît Sevens (using Claude) with discovering and reporting the flaw.

"Email is the easiest door into any company, and this flaw turns one opened file into a stolen identity," Jack Bicer, director of vulnerability research at Action1, said. "A captured hash can let an attacker sign in as the victim, read their data, and move to other systems they can reach."

"The Moderate label undersells this one. Attackers are already exploiting it, it needs only one click on an email file, and it hits Outlook, which nearly every organization runs. A stolen hash can open doors far beyond the inbox."

That said, Redmond has not attributed the activity to a particular threat actor or provided technical details on how the vulnerability is being exploited in the wild. The advisory also doesn't spell out whether the discovery came before or after attackers began exploiting the flaw.

The development has prompted the U.S. U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to add the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fix by November 24, 2026.

Some other vulnerabilities of note include a number of remote code execution flaws impacting Windows Search (CVE-2026-116928), Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (CVE-2026-119958), Windows Schannel (CVE-2026-119952), Windows Virtual Filtering Platform (CVE-2026-95962), and Windows Xbox Live Networking Service (CVE-2026-112967), as well as a privilege escalation flaw in Azure OpenAI (CVE-2026-119990).

This attack pattern continues to be attractive to phishing operators and initial access brokers because it converts document or message delivery into reliable code execution, bypassing the user-action barrier that many enterprises treat as a training backstop.
Identity platform components face elevated risk this month with Critical flaws in both Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) and Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS). CVE-2026-119958 enables RCE against LDAP, while CVE-2026-118146 and CVE-2026-118148 target AD DS with RCE and elevation-of-privilege attack paths, respectively. These protocols underpin domain authentication and authorization for every joined workstation and server; successful exploitation of either can cascade to domain-wide compromise. Similar identity fabric vulnerabilities have historically been targeted by advanced adversaries seeking persistent access to enterprise environments.
Windows Hyper-V sees an unusually high concentration of privilege escalation vulnerabilities this month, with eight CVEs spanning multiple flaw classes. CVE-2026-113753, CVE-2026-113856, and CVE-2026-113860 all enable elevation of privilege within the hypervisor boundary. Hyper-V underpins Azure compute infrastructure and endpoint features such as Windows Sandbox, Credential Guard, and other Virtualization-Based Security capabilities, so the exposure extends beyond dedicated virtualization hosts to ordinary Windows endpoints with these features enabled.

The unauthenticated network-reachable RCE cluster spans 14 CVEs this month, with Windows Message Queuing (MSMQ) vulnerabilities such as CVE-2026-109459 and CVE-2026-116710 representing exposure on any system with MSMQ enabled. CVE-2026-125926 - Server-side request forgery in the server registration and update API in mcp-gateway-registry

Bulletin ID: 2026-180-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/11/2026 13:00 PM PST

Description:

mcp-gateway-registry is an open-source registry and gateway for Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers that centralizes discovery, access control, and proxying of registered MCP tool assets. We identified CVE-2026-125926, a server-side request forgery issue in how the registry validates the upstream address of a registered server.

An authenticated user with permission to register or modify a server could configure an upstream address that caused the gateway to send requests to services on the deployment's internal network. In some cases the gateway returned those responses to the user.

Impacted versions: >= v1.0.3 AND <= 1.34.0

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in mcp-gateway-registry version 1.35.0. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Note on version sequencing: a separate and unrelated issue in this product's external management API was addressed in version 1.25.0. A deployment running 1.25.0 or later carries that fix, but remains affected by the issue described here until it runs version 1.35.0 or later.

Post-upgrade actions:

Version 1.35.0 validates server upstream addresses when a server is registered or modified. It leaves server configurations stored before the upgrade unchanged. Customers who ran an affected version should take the following steps after upgrading:

Review the upstream addresses of registered servers, and correct or remove any address you did not intend.
Review application logs from the period an affected version was deployed for unexpected server registrations and changes.
If the registry runs with an attached cloud role and the log review cannot rule out unexpected activity, review that role's activity and rotate its credentials.

Workarounds:

The following measures limit risk for deployments that cannot yet upgrade. They do not replace the post-upgrade actions above:

Limit the permission to register and modify servers to trusted accounts.
Restrict outbound network access from the registry and auth-server components to the destinations they need.
On Amazon EC2, require IMDSv2. Grant the role attached to each component only the permissions it needs.

CVE-2026-100307 - Missing authorization on the external management API in mcp-gateway-registry enables privilege escalation to registry administrator

Bulletin ID: 2026-179-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/11/2026 12:30 PM PST

Description:

Amazon mcp-gateway-registry is an open-source registry and gateway for Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers that centralizes discovery, access control, and proxying of registered MCP tool assets. We identified CVE-2026-100307, a missing-authorization issue in the external management API.

The /api/servers/* management endpoints authenticated the caller but did not perform role-based or permission-based authorization. As a result, an authenticated low-privileged remote user could submit a crafted group import request to POST /api/servers/groups/import that mapped their own identity-provider group to the registry administrator scope. Because administrator status is derived per request, the escalation took effect on the caller's next request with no re-authentication, granting administrative control over every registered gateway asset.

Impacted versions: >= 1.0.9 AND <= 1.24.7

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in mcp-gateway-registry version 1.25.0 (released 2026-06-27). We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Post-upgrade actions:

Version 1.25.0 enforces authorization on the write path. It does not modify group definitions that were written before the upgrade, and it does not invalidate credentials that were read before the upgrade. A privileged group mapping created through the affected endpoints continues to confer administrator access after the upgrade. Customers who ran an affected version (>= 1.0.9, <= 1.24.7) should complete the following steps after upgrading, using the period during which an affected version was deployed as the review period.

Review the scope store. In the mcp_scopes DocumentDB collection, inspect each group_mappings entry for a mapping to mcp-registry-admin or another privileged scope, and each ui_permissions entry that grants a mutating action to all. Remove any grant that was not created by an administrator. This step removes administrator access that otherwise persists after the upgrade.
Review application HTTP logs. For the review period, search for POST /api/servers/groups/import requests from non-administrator accounts, and for requests to the sibling routes /api/servers/groups/create, /api/servers/groups/add, /api/servers/groups/remove, and /api/servers/groups/delete, and to the affected server-mutation routes. Correlate any result with subsequent /api/servers/* requests from the same identity to determine which resources were modified.

title: MSP Process security incident creates customer tenant risk
text:
November 11, 2026

Security intelligence

MSP Process security incident creates customer tenant risk

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

MSP Process recently disclosed a security incident involving unauthorized access to infrastructure containing application credentials, administrator refresh tokens, and Granular Delegated Admin Privileges (GDAP) relationship data used by Microsoft administrative integrations.

Public reporting indicates compromised MSP Process credentials were used in customer environments. Reported activity included authentication attempts across multiple tenants and, in at least one investigated environment, the creation of additional credentials, role assignments, and service accounts intended to maintain access.

The primary concern, beyond the exposure of the original credentials, is that additional credentials, permissions, accounts, or other persistence mechanisms could have been established before containment actions were completed.

Threat summary
On November 7, MSP Process notified partners that a threat actor who gained access to one of its internal servers had access to a company storage account between approximately 09:56 UTC and 14:40 UTC.
The storage contained application client IDs and client secrets used by MSP Process integrations, administrator refresh tokens associated with connected services, and Granular Delegated Admin Privileges (GDAP) relationship information.
MSP Process removed the threat actor’s access, rotated platform credentials, and disabled the compromised storage key at 19:05 UTC that day.
The incident affects MSP Process apps used for identity management and tenant administration, including Authenticator, Password Reset, and Contacts Sync. These apps connect to customer environments through Microsoft Partner Center’s administrative relationships and have permissions to manage user accounts, authentication methods, and applications across connected tenants.
Following the disclosure, MSP Process reported that the threat actor also accessed infrastructure supporting its Microsoft Partner Center integrations, including application credentials and access tokens used by those services. The company disabled password reset, multifactor authentication (MFA) reset, user unlock, and authenticator verification functionality, engaged an external incident response firm, and expanded its remediation guidance to all customers. The guidance includes rotating API keys and credentials for integrations such as PSA, RMM, messaging, Teams, and mail.
The significance of the incident lies in these permissions. Possession of a valid client secret allows an application to authenticate directly to Microsoft cloud services without user interaction, an administrator sign-in, or an MFA challenge.
Third-party reporting indicates the exposed credentials were used in customer environments, with authentication attempts across 47 environments. Most activity was limited to brief authentication events. In one investigated environment, the threat actor reportedly granted additional permissions to the MSP Process application, added credentials to dozens of applications, created service accounts, accessed data, and re-enabled accounts disabled during response efforts. Attempts to use exposed administrator refresh tokens reportedly failed. The activity has not been publicly attributed to a specific threat actor.
Analysis
To perform password resets, MFA administration, and other delegated-administration functions, MSP Process applications rely on Microsoft Graph application permissions that allow them to act independently of a signed-in user.
Depending on the feature enabled, documented permissions include:

Application.ReadWrite.All, which allows credentials to be added to other applications within the tenant.

title: AI Is Both Target and Tool for Threat Actors
text:
PUBLISHED ON 11 NOV 2026

Insikt Group®

Summary
Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled attacks are accelerating, with AI as both a target and a force multiplier. Of the 103 AI-enabled incidents analyzed for this report, most involve AI accelerating familiar attack types (supply-chain compromise, phishing, extortion) and making them more convincing. The use of AI is evident throughout the attack lifecycle, though full automation remains rare. Note: The period of analysis for this report is between July 31, 2025 and July 31, 2026.
Developer tools are a prime target. Because AI coding assistants and proxy packages often have privileged access to credentials and code, threat actors use them as footholds for mass credential theft and lateral movement across downstream environments.
State-sponsored actors are beginning to experiment with agentic capabilities. Most of the state-sponsored activity in this report falls within Recorded Future’s AI Malware Maturity Model Level 2–3 (AI-assisted malware development), with one notable exception: a campaign against Taiwanese government entities that employed up to eight AI agents with limited human intervention.
Fully autonomous attacks remain rare, likely for both maturity and operational-risk reasons. Human oversight still appears necessary for reliable outcomes, which may limit the full automation of cyberattacks, especially in sensitive operations where an agent's error can have outsized consequences.
This restraint is unlikely to hold. As agentic techniques mature and diffuse across the threat landscape, autonomous and orchestrated campaigns are likely to become more frequent, alongside a growing underground market for illicit access to commercial models and rising "noise" from low-level automated intrusions that complicate the detection of serious threats.

Figure 1: Five trends in offensive use of AI (Source: Recorded Future)

AnalysisThe DataOffensive use of AI remains a serious concern for cyber defenders, especially as recent advances in AI capabilities are increasing the risk of autonomous attacks. To better understand the risk, Insikt Group identified 103 incidents between July 31, 2025, and July 31, 2026, in which AI was part of a malicious campaign. To qualify, events had to be:
Documented incidents that are searchable in the Recorded Future intelligence graph
Confirmed as using AI as the attack vector, tool, or target
Carried out by malicious actors in the wild, not as proofs-of-concept or security research
Of the 103 incidents identified, 32 involved the use of AI in malware or to orchestrate offensive cyber operations. These incidents were categorized along Recorded Future’s AI Malware Maturity Model (AIM3), which evaluates how AI is used in malicious or offensive software. The remaining 71 incidents were sorted into one of four categories that best describe how AI was abused:
Targeting AI systems, infrastructure, or data: Attacks where AI platforms, tools, or companies are the direct target rather than a means of attack
AI as lure or delivery vector: Social engineering that uses AI's current hype and popularity as bait to deliver malware, rather than exploiting anything technical about AI itself
AI-assisted deception, fraud, or influence: AI used as a tool by the attacker to make fraud, phishing, or influence operations more convincing and personalized to the target audience
Abuse or hijacking of AI agents/services: Misuse of legitimate AI systems' own capabilities, rather than a single dominant technique

Roughly one-third of the incidents across both datasets are financially motivated. title: CopperHound: open-source attack-path analysis for AD, ADCS and Entra ID, written in Rust
text:
CopperHound
Open-source Active Directory, ADCS and Entra ID / Azure attack-path analysis,
built in Rust for very large environments. CopperHound ingests SharpHound,
bloodhound-python, ldapdomaindump and AzureHound output, raw LDIF dumps and
Sysinternals AD Explorer snapshots into a memory-mapped graph store and runs
path, exposure and CHQL queries directly on it, with no graph database. One
container serves the web UI and REST API.

Screenshots use fabricated demo data (scripts/demo_data.py).
Documentation: User guide · Deployment ·
Data sources · REST API · CHQL ·
Edge reference · Performance ·
Architecture
Quick start (Docker)
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose logs copperhound | grep "Initial admin password"

Open http://127.0.0.1:8090, sign in as admin, drop your SharpHound /
AzureHound .zip or .json files on the Data tab and press Rebuild
graph. COPPERHOUND_ADMIN_PASSWORD sets the password, and
COPPERHOUND_PORT / COPPERHOUND_HOST change the published address (default
127.0.0.1:8090, so it can run next to BloodHound on 8080).
No data yet? python scripts/demo_data.py demo/ writes a fabricated
environment (AD, ADCS and Entra ID with deliberate weaknesses) to upload; see
Try it with demo data.
Without Docker: cd web && npm ci && npm run build, then
cargo run --release -- serve (defaults: 127.0.0.1:8080, data in ./data,
UI from ./web/dist).
Accounts, API tokens, the watch folder, scheduled reports, change alerts, HTTPS
and single sign-on (OpenID Connect, SAML 2.0): docs/DEPLOYMENT.md.
Risk analysis
Computed in the background after every ingest:

Attack-path findings — 30 finding types across AD, ADCS, Entra ID and
hybrid (DCSync outside Tier Zero, control of Tier Zero, rights of broad groups,
delegation to Tier Zero, ESC escalations, tenant-takeover Graph permissions,
synced accounts holding Entra Tier Zero roles, …), each with severity,
impact, remediation guidance and MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Every edge finding
is measured: "fixing this removes N principals' paths to Tier Zero",
computed by re-running the exposure analysis without its edges.
What-if simulation — remove any set of edges, edge kinds or nodes (or add
targets) and see before/after exposure per kind, instantly.
Remediation planner — a dominator tree over every attack path finds the
choke object whose fix cuts the most principals off from the zone
entirely. The plan is recomputed after each step, so the cumulative
reduction curve is exact. Members of zone groups are treated
as part of the zone, so it never proposes "remove the admins from Domain
Admins".
Remediation hand-off — turn fix-list edges or plan steps into a
PowerShell script (one suggested command per edge, objects named by SID /
object id) or into Jira issues, ServiceNow records or signed webhook events
with the guidance and command for each edge.
Privilege zones — define your own target sets with a CHQL selector
("Tier 1 servers", "Finance file servers", …) and get exposure, choke points
and remediation plans for each. In a zone's member review you certify the
members that belong and revoke ones the rule picked up by mistake (they drop
out of the zone); new matches show as pending.
Posture over time — one snapshot per ingest (exposure %, findings by
severity, per-finding counts) and a diff between any two snapshots listing
exactly which finding items appeared or were resolved.

CLI equivalents: copperhound findings corp.chg, copperhound plan corp.chg --steps 10.
Web UI
A WebGL graph canvas (sigma.js) with search, pathfinding, node details, "How was
this derived?" for every derived edge, the CHQL editor and query library, and
pages for findings, remediation, zones, posture, reports, data and
administration. Walkthrough with screenshots: docs/USER_GUIDE.md.
CHQL
A read-only Cypher dialect compiled to native graph operations — multiple
patterns and MATCH clauses, OPTIONAL MATCH, WITH, aggregation,
ORDER BY/SKIP/LIMIT, UNION, undirected and variable-length hops, path
functions and pattern […]

Authors

Boris Trefilov

In recent years, cyberthreats have increasingly taken a hybrid approach, combining time-tested techniques for advancing through infrastructure, modern methods of evading network filters, and automation powered by large language models. This is also the approach of Citrus Ransomware, a previously undocumented group whose toolset includes VLESS tunnels (used to disguise traffic as regular HTTPS) and a ransomware Trojan from the Sn00py family. The attackers also integrate LLMs (large language models) into the process of infrastructure compromise.
In this article, we review the tactics and techniques the group used in recent incidents.
Initial Access: attacks through contractors
The attackers gain initial access to victims’ infrastructure through compromised contractors. They use credentials stolen from these contractors’ employees to connect to corporate VPNs or directly to internet-facing terminal servers over RDP.
Execution: commands, LLMs, and Impacket
The attackers run commands on compromised systems through the standard Windows command interpreter and PowerShell. As the attack progresses, they create and run PowerShell scripts, batch files, and commands generated by LLMs. One example of the latter is the commands below, which disable the account of one of the administrators.

Comment translation
# Disable account
# Verify result
Both commands come with comments, something attackers rarely bother with, so the comments very likely point to LLM use. And the models did more than generate commands. The attackers also produced full scripts, complete with the comments typical of LLM output.

# Creating background tasks for each computer with a thread limit
# Concurrent task limit control
# Quick ping
The fragment above comes from a script Citrus used to enumerate active user sessions on domain systems.
Besides LLMs, the attackers use atexec, a classic tool from the Impacket collection, to create scheduled tasks that run commands on hosts:

When the group compromises 1C:Enterprise servers, it uses external data processors (1C-Shell) to run commands.

On systems that are not regularly rebooted, such as terminal servers, they sometimes run their tools without establishing persistence at all.

In every case we know of, the contractor domain account used for initial access had very limited privileges, so the attackers tried to escalate them.

Arctic Wolf saw attackers use the AntiFox pentest platform to hit IIS servers and AWS accounts.

Arctic Wolf Labs has published research on attackers using AntiFox, an open-source, Chinese-language agentic penetration testing platform. These frameworks chain attack steps together with little human effort. In several intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were tied to confirmed attacks on internet-facing web services and the AWS environments behind them.

Two entry points showed up. In some cases, the attackers got into a public IIS application, though Arctic Wolf couldn’t identify the vulnerability. In others, they started with a valid AWS credential obtained by means nobody knows.

“Arctic Wolf is tracking the emerging use of self-hosted agentic penetration testing frameworks, including AntiFox, from public cloud infrastructure.” states the report published by Arctic Wolf, “In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments.”

The IIS attacks followed a similar pattern. The IIS worker process, w3wp.exe, created an ASPX web shell and then ran commands to gather information about the system. The attackers checked the user account, listed files in the application folder, reviewed file permissions using icacls and tested whether they could write files to the website’s main folder.

They then used PowerShell to read the web.config file, looking for database connection details and application settings. They also checked folders containing debug and error logs. title: How to Export Logs with Amazon Athena
text:
En

LogTotal HOWTO

November 11, 2026
3 min read

Athena doesn’t store logs itself. It queries log files in S3, such as CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, load balancer and WAF logs, through tables you define. Normal query results are saved as CSV in your results bucket. To get JSON instead, wrap the query in UNLOAD … WITH (format = ‘JSON’): Athena writes newline-delimited JSON to an S3 prefix, and you download it.

Plenty of AWS teams keep months of logs in S3 and query them with Athena rather than shipping everything to a SIEM. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get a slice out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

Permissions. You need to run Athena queries (athena:StartQueryExecution and related), read the table definitions in Glue, read the source bucket, and write to an export bucket. Add kms:Decrypt if the logs are encrypted with KMS.

Know the table and its partitions. A CloudTrail table is usually partitioned by region and date, either with partition projection or with partitions you’ve added. Athena bills by data scanned, so filter on partitions every time. A query without them can scan years of logs.

A workgroup. Athena runs queries in a workgroup with a results location. UNLOAD writes to its own target, but the workgroup still needs to be set up.

Export with UNLOAD

UNLOAD (  SELECT *  FROM cloudtrail_logs  WHERE region = 'eu-west-1'    AND day = '2026/10/19'    AND useridentity.arn LIKE '%suspicious-user%')TO 's3://my-athena-exports/ct-1019/'WITH (format = 'JSON', compression = 'NONE')

Adapt the partition columns (region, day) to your table definition. The target prefix must be empty.

From the command line:

QID=$(aws athena start-query-execution –work-group primary \  –query-string “$(cat unload.sql)” \  –query ‘QueryExecutionId’ –output text)# wait until SUCCEEDEDuntil [ “$(aws athena get-query-execution –query-execution-id “$QID” \  –query ‘QueryExecution.Status.State’ –output text)” = “SUCCEEDED” ]; do sleep 5; doneaws s3 cp s3://my-athena-exports/ct-1019/ ./ct-1019/ –recursivezcat -f ./ct-1019/* > ct_1019.jsonl

zcat -f handles both compressed and uncompressed output, in case compression was left at the default. If the query fails, the wait loop never ends. Check for FAILED too if you script this regularly.

Why not get-query-results? It works, but it returns rows as lists of strings, 1,000 per page, which you then have to stitch back into objects. UNLOAD gives you clean JSON in one step.

Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file.

Sanitize.

Review.

When it goes wrong

SymptomLikely causeFixQuery scans terabytesNo partition filterFilter on the partition columnsError about the output locationTarget prefix isn’t emptyUse a new prefixAccess DeniedMissing S3, Glue or KMS permissionCheck each one; KMS is the usual suspectZero rowsPartitions not loaded, or the wrong partition formatCheck partition projection or run MSCK REPAIR TABLEOutput files won’t open as textGZIP compressionUse zcat, or set compression = ‘NONE’

FAQ Is this the same as Amazon Security Lake?Security Lake uses Athena too, but with its own OCSF tables and Lake Formation permissions.Can I export raw CloudTrail files instead?Yes. If you only need whole days, copying the files from S3 is simpler. Athena earns its keep when you need to filter.

How to Export Databricks Logs
text:
En

LogTotal HOWTO

November 11, 2026
3 min read

As with Snowflake, “Databricks logs” can mean security data you keep in Delta tables, or Databricks’ own audit log in the system.access.audit system table. The simplest export for both is a notebook cell. Query with Spark SQL, write the result as JSON to a Unity Catalog volume, then download it with the Databricks CLI. Spark writes newline-delimited JSON, so the files are ready for upload.

Databricks is increasingly used as a security data lake, and its audit log matters in its own right: who logged in, who created tokens, who changed permissions. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get the data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

Access. Reading system.access.audit needs the system schema enabled for your metastore and a SELECT grant from an account or metastore admin. For your own tables, you need the usual Unity Catalog grants.

A volume to write to. You need a Unity Catalog volume you can write to, for example /Volumes/security/exports/logtotal, and the Databricks CLI configured on your machine.

Compute. A notebook needs a cluster or serverless compute. Filter by date so you don’t scan more than you need.

Export from a notebook

(spark.sql("""    SELECT *    FROM system.access.audit    WHERE event_date = '2026-10-19'      AND action_name IN ('login', 'tokenLogin', 'generateDbToken')""") .write.mode("overwrite") .json("/Volumes/security/exports/logtotal/audit_20261019"))

Spark writes several part-*.json files plus marker files. Download and combine them:

databricks fs cp -r dbfs:/Volumes/security/exports/logtotal/audit_20261019 ./audit_20261019cat ./audit_20261019/part-*.json > databricks_audit_20261019.jsonl

For your own security tables, change the query: select from your table and filter on its timestamp column.

Without a notebook, the SQL Statement Execution API can run the same query on a SQL warehouse and return JSON. Rows come back as arrays, with the column names in a separate manifest, so you need an extra step to turn them into objects. For anything sizable, the notebook route is simpler.

What to look for in the audit log

Look at logins and token logins from unusual IP addresses, new personal access tokens, changes to permissions and group membership, and workspace or cluster configuration changes outside normal hours. Downloads of notebooks or results in bulk are worth a look too.

Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file.

Sanitize.

Review.

When it goes wrong

SymptomLikely causeFixsystem.access.audit not foundSystem schema not enabledAsk an account admin to enable itPermission denied on the system tableNo SELECT grantAsk a metastore admin for the grantCan’t write to the volumeMissing WRITE VOLUMEUse a volume you can write toDownload includes _SUCCESS and other filesSpark marker filesCombine only part-*.jsonHuge, slow queryNo date filterFilter on event_date

FAQ Is the audit log also delivered to cloud storage?Workspaces can deliver audit logs to your own storage as well. If that’s set up, you can copy those files directly.Does this work on workspaces without Unity Catalog?The system tables need Unity Catalog. Older workspaces rely on audit log delivery to storage, and you write to DBFS paths instead of volumes.

title: How to Export BigQuery Logs
text:
En

LogTotal HOWTO

November 11, 2026
3 min read

When security logs sit in BigQuery (from a Cloud Logging sink, a Google Workspace export or your own pipeline), export them with EXPORT DATA. It writes newline-delimited JSON to a Cloud Storage bucket, and you download that. For small results, bq query –format=json prints the rows directly. Either way, filter on the table’s time or partition column first, because BigQuery bills by data scanned.

BigQuery is where many Google Cloud teams keep log history long after Cloud Logging’s default retention has passed. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get a slice out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

Permissions. You need to run jobs (BigQuery Job User), read the dataset (BigQuery Data Viewer), and write to the export bucket.

Know the tables. A Cloud Logging sink to BigQuery creates tables named after the logs, for example cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity, often partitioned by timestamp. Workspace exports have their own schema.

Check the cost first. Add –dry_run to a bq query to see how many bytes it would scan. If the number makes you wince, add a tighter time filter.

Option 1: EXPORT DATA to Cloud Storage

EXPORT DATA OPTIONS (  uri = 'gs://my-bq-exports/audit-20261019/*.json',  format = 'JSON',  overwrite = true) ASSELECT *FROM `my-project.audit_logs.cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity`WHERE timestamp >= TIMESTAMP('2026-10-19') AND timestamp < TIMESTAMP('2026-10-20');

The URI needs a wildcard (*), because BigQuery may write several files. Download and combine them:

gcloud storage cp 'gs://my-bq-exports/audit-20261019/*' ./audit-20261019/cat ./audit-20261019/*.json > bq_audit_20261019.jsonl

Option 2: bq query for small results

bq query --nouse_legacy_sql --format=json --max_rows=10000 \  'SELECT * FROM `my-project.audit_logs.cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity`   WHERE timestamp >= TIMESTAMP("2026-10-19") AND timestamp < TIMESTAMP("2026-10-20")' \  > bq_audit_small.jsonjq -c '.[]' bq_audit_small.json > bq_audit_small.jsonl

–format=json prints a JSON array, which jq flattens to one row per line.

Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file.

Sanitize.

Review.

When it goes wrong

SymptomLikely causeFixQuery scans the whole tableNo filter on the partition or time columnFilter on timestamp (or _PARTITIONTIME)EXPORT DATA fails on the URINo wildcard in the URIUse …/*.jsonPermission denied writing to the bucketMissing Storage object create rightsGrant write access on the bucketbq output cut at 100 rowsDefault –max_rowsSet –max_rows, or use EXPORT DATANested fields look oddRepeated and nested columns keep their structureExpected; it’s still valid JSON

FAQ Is this the same as exporting from Cloud Logging?No. Cloud Logging has its own export. This guide is for logs that already live in BigQuery tables.Can I export a whole table without a queryYes: bq extract –destination_format NEWLINE_DELIMITED_JSON copies a table or a partition to Cloud Storage. For investigations, a filtered query is usually better.

title: CVE-2026-124194: Microsoft Outlook Zero-Day Exploited to Steal NTLM Hashes
text:
Microsoft has patched CVE-2026-124194, an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook that can expose a user’s NTLMv2 authentication information when a specially crafted message file is opened. Microsoft classifies the issue as a spoofing vulnerability and rates it Moderate with a CVSS 3.1 score of 6.5.

The vulnerability allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to send a malicious message file and convince a victim to open it in an affected Outlook version. Outlook can then connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the external-content warning users would normally expect. During that connection, Windows may expose NTLMv2 authentication information that can potentially be abused to impersonate the victim.

Contact Sales

Microsoft confirmed that CVE-2026-124194 has already been exploited in attacks. However, the company has not disclosed the threat actors involved, the scale of the campaign, victim organizations, delivery infrastructure, or whether the stolen authentication material has been used for subsequent lateral movement or account compromise.

The flaw was addressed as part of Microsoft’s November 2026 Patch Tuesday release on November 10. Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Microsoft Office LTSC 2021, and Microsoft Office LTSC 2024 on both 32-bit and x64 systems.

CISA added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 10, confirming evidence of active exploitation and establishing November 24, 2026 as the remediation deadline for applicable U.S. federal agencies.

Security teams can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to operationalize threat intelligence, identify suspicious Outlook and NTLM activity, and accelerate detection engineering and threat hunting across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Detect CVE-2026-124194 by correlating Outlook activity with unexpected outbound SMB connections, NTLM authentication attempts to external systems, suspicious message-file execution, and subsequent credential or identity abuse.

Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added.

CVE-2026-124194 analysis

CVE-2026-124194 affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Microsoft Office LTSC 2021, and Microsoft Office LTSC 2024. Microsoft assigns the flaw a CVSS 3.1 score of 6.5 with the vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N, reflecting remote accessibility, low attack complexity, no required attacker privileges, required user interaction, and high confidentiality impact.

The vulnerability is classified under CWE-356, Product UI Does Not Warn User of Unsafe Actions. In practical terms, Outlook does not display the warning that should normally alert a user before the application accesses potentially dangerous external content.

Exploitation begins with a specially crafted Outlook message file delivered to the target. The attacker does not need an account on the victim’s system or Microsoft 365 tenant, but the victim must open the malicious file. Microsoft specifically states that the Preview Pane is not an attack vector, meaning simply displaying the message in Outlook’s preview interface is not sufficient.

Once the file is opened, Outlook can initiate a connection to a network location controlled by the attacker without presenting the usual external-content warning.

This is significant because Windows environments can automatically attempt NTLM authentication when accessing remote resources. The resulting challenge-response exchange can expose the user’s NTLMv2 authentication hash to the remote server.

An NTLMv2 hash is not the user’s plaintext password. However, possession of authentication material can create several follow-on risks depending on the environment and the attacker’s capabilities. […]

title: Online Casino Serves Malicious Python SDK
text:
Jump to sectionThe OpenSourceMalware team discovered a malicious PyPI package called aurum-pay, and it looks like exactly what it claims to be. It’s a payment SDK for an online casino, with documented methods for deposits, payouts, refunds, balances, and signed webhooks, and those methods work. The casino’s website works too. But the first time an application makes a real payment request through the SDK, it quietly fetches a command from the casino’s domain and runs it. On Linux, that command installs a remote access trojan that gives its operator a persistent shell on the host.Click here to see the aurum-pay threat report. As of the publishing of this article, both the package and user account are still live on PyPI.A few things make this one worth a closer look.The loader waits for normal use: There’s no install hook, no import-time code, and no encoded blob. Installing aurum-pay or creating a client does nothing. The malicious code sits inside the same method that sends legitimate API calls, so it only fires when an application is actually using the package.The brand is part of the attack: The package points to aurum-casino[.]com for its homepage and documentation, and that site presents a functioning casino. The College of Healthcare Information Management Executives and 17 health systems are urging federal regulators to not water-down providers' ability to verify patient authorization for PHI disclosures to third-party apps. (Image: Getty Images)

A coalition of healthcare organizations is urging U.S. federal regulators not to adopt potential changes to the HIPAA Privacy Rule that they say could restrict providers from verifying whether patients have authorized third-party applications to access their sensitive medical information.See Also: Your Face Is Your Boarding Pass: How Biometric Identity Is Redefining the Way We Travel
Such restrictions could increase the risk of privacy and security breaches while exposing healthcare providers to civil liability and regulatory scrutiny, the College of Healthcare Information Management Executives, or CHIME, and 17 healthcare organizations contend in a Nov. 10 letter to U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
The letter was also copied to several HHS officials, including Paula Stannard, director of the department's Office for Civil Rights, which oversees HIPAA rulemaking and enforcement.
Besides CHIME, a professional association of healthcare IT executives and organizations signing the letter include AdventHealth, Baptist Health in Jacksonville, Florida, Bryan Health, Claiborne Memorial Medical Center, Cleveland Clinic, Fisher-Titus Medical Center, Fulton County Health Center, Genesis HealthCare System, Helio Health, MedStar Health, OrthoVirginia, RiverSpring Living, Sharp HealthCare, the University of Kansas Health System and Medical Center, Trinity Health, Trinity Rehabilitation Services and Wooster Community Hospital.
The organizations warn that the forthcoming final HIPAA Privacy Rule could include provisions that "categorically prohibit" healthcare providers from independently confirming whether patients have authorized third-party applications to receive their protected health information, or PHI.
They are also concerned that HHS could treat some identity verification credentials as sufficient to permit applications to obtain patient information without allowing providers to independently confirm the scope or validity of patient authorization.
In 2021, during the final days of President Donald Trump's first term, HHS OCR issued a proposed update to the HIPAA Privacy Rule aimed at strengthening care coordination, improving patient access to health information and eliminating "unnecessary regulatory burdens." (See: HHS Reveals Proposed Changes to HIPAA Privacy Rule)
The 357-page proposal remained largely dormant during the Biden administration, but HHS OCR is now expected to release a final rule before the end of the year.
Current Trump administration officials are said to be pushing for changes to the final rule that differ from those formally proposed in 2021, a source told ISMG. Those changes include provisions that would prohibit healthcare providers from independently confirming whether patients have authorized third-party applications to receive their PHI.
"The 2021 NPRM expressly preserved covered entities' ability to employ reasonable verification measures, signaling that the proposed restrictions were intended to address unreasonable barriers rather than eliminate legitimate safeguards," CHIME wrote.
The organizations argue that a categorical prohibition on reasonable authorization checks would go substantially beyond the original proposal, potentially exposing providers to liability while increasing privacy and security risks for patients.

Shadow AI Is a Training Problem Before a Tool Problem
Security Teams Need AI Literacy and Governance to Reduce Employee-Driven Risk

Gilles Castro

•
November 11, 2026

Image: Shutterstock
Cybersecurity professionals have spent years learning how to defend networks, applications and endpoints from external attackers. But shadow use of artificial intelligence tools changes that equation.See Also: Your Face Is Your Boarding Pass: How Biometric Identity Is Redefining the Way We Travel
The people creating risk may already have legitimate access to the company's systems and data. They may also believe they're simply finding a faster way to work.
That makes shadow AI as much an education problem as a technology problem.
A recent O'Reilly Media survey of 209 security professionals found employee AI use ranked as a leading concern. Practitioners worried most about workers putting company data into AI tools.
AI-generated phishing, in contrast, was the AI attack practitioners encountered most often. Yet only about one-fourth ranked it among their top concerns.
That's a big problem for educators.
The Risk Has Moved Closer to the User
Traditional security training often teaches employees to recognize external threats. They learn to spot suspicious links, protect credentials and report phishing attempts.
Shadow AI requires another layer of judgment.
An employee might paste source code into a generative AI service to troubleshoot a problem. Another might upload customer information to summarize a document.
A third might provide strategic plans to an AI assistant while preparing a presentation.
Each employee may have a legitimate business goal. The risk comes from where the information goes, how the service handles it and whether company policy covers the interaction.
That means security awareness programs must move beyond simple warnings about unauthorized tools.
Employees need to understand data classification, approved AI services and the types of information they can share. They also need clear alternatives when public tools aren't appropriate.
AI Literacy Must Become a Security Skill
Security teams also need deeper AI literacy. Professionals don't need to become machine learning engineers. They do need to understand how generative AI changes data exposure, access decisions and user behavior.
They should know how employees use these systems in real workflows. That knowledge helps security teams design controls people can follow instead of rules they work around.
Training should prepare practitioners to answer practical questions:
Which information can employees provide to an AI service? Which AI tools has the organization approved? How should teams evaluate new AI applications? Who owns decisions about acceptable AI risk? How can security teams detect risky AI use without blocking productive work?
These questions require more than technical controls. They require policy design, communication and an understanding of business priorities.
Security Education Must Connect Cyber Risk With Business Risk
The shift extends beyond shadow AI.
A recent Gartner survey of 308 enterprise risk management leaders found that four of the five highest-ranked emerging risks involved AI.
AI strategy miscalculation ranked third. AI-driven competitive displacement ranked fourth, while the AI workforce preparedness gap ranked fifth.
Those findings should influence how we prepare cybersecurity professionals.
Security teams can no longer treat AI only as another attack surface. AI adoption also affects workforce readiness, competitive strategy and business investment.

The scope-change flag (S:C) and high confidentiality impact (C:H) reflect that the vulnerable server can be coerced into reaching resources and trust boundaries beyond its own security authority — most notably cloud instance metadata endpoints and internal-only services. Technical Analysis
Vulnerability class
CVE-2026-76900 is a classic stored (second-order) Server-Side Request Forgery, mapped to CWE-918. The defining characteristic is a validation asymmetry: the application implements SSRF controls on one code path (testConnect) but not on the code path that actually performs the production request.
Data flow (as described by the NVD description)
The vulnerable chain is:

Storage — ApprovalResourceService.sendWebHook reads a webHookUrl value from stored approval-node configuration. This value is populated by a user through POST /approval-flow/add and persisted as part of the approval-flow definition.
Propagation — The stored URL is passed through ApprovalFlowService.updateApprovalPostField.
Sink — The URL is delivered to HttpClientUtils, which performs the outbound HTTP request server-side.
Trigger — The request fires when POST /approval-action/approve executes the approval action, invoking the webhook send path.

The critical detail is that the testConnect path — an optional connectivity test — applies SSRF validation, but the sendWebHook path does not. An attacker therefore only needs to bypass validation on the storage endpoint (which, per the description, does not appear to enforce it for the webhook send flow), not on the execution path. This is a common engineering failure: developers validate the "test" button but forget that the same user-controlled URL is later dereferenced by background or transaction-triggered code.

The URL is stored and re-used later, decoupling the attacker's request from the outbound connection.

Unverified dark web claim. This report is based on a post observed on a dark web forum. Yazoul Security has not independently verified the authenticity of this claim.
Claim Summary
On or around November 10, 2026, a ransomware group calling itself “BYOD” allegedly posted Toyota (toyota.jp) to its dark web leak site. The group claims to have exfiltrated personal information including full names, email addresses, physical addresses, phone numbers, and dates of birth, along with data referencing “kiosk devices.” No data volume was disclosed.
In its posting, the threat actor purportedly acknowledged that Toyota isolated “a lot” of the intrusion but claims “a few cracks” allowed access. The group states it will “take you down” once communication is established. This language is consistent with standard double extortion pressure tactics and should be treated with skepticism until independently corroborated.
Threat Actor Profile
BYOD is a low-profile ransomware operation with no publicly documented track record, no confirmed victim count, and no established tooling attribution. Open-source research returns no reliable references describing the group’s malware family, initial access vectors, or infrastructure. This absence of public reporting is a significant credibility gap.
Because BYOD has no verifiable history, analysts cannot assess whether the group possesses genuine capability or is a rebrand, a copycat, or an opportunistic actor recycling another operation’s branding. Groups with thin or nonexistent track records frequently exaggerate breach scope to manufacture urgency. Until independent evidence emerges, the group’s claims should be weighted accordingly. No YARA rules or detection signatures specific to BYOD are publicly available at this time; defenders should rely on general ransomware detection guidance and behavioral monitoring rather than actor-specific indicators.
Alleged Data Exposure
According to the threat actor, the purported dataset includes:

Full names
Email addresses
Physical addresses
Phone numbers
Dates of birth
References to “kiosk devices”

The group did not disclose record counts, sample files, or proof-of-compromise artifacts in the portion of the posting reviewed. No data samples, credentials, or access details are reproduced here by policy. The mention of kiosk devices, if accurate, could imply exposure of endpoint or point-of-service systems rather than core corporate databases, but this remains speculation.
Potential Impact
If the claim is substantiated, exposed personal data could enable phishing, identity fraud, and targeted social engineering against employees or customers. Manufacturing environments are attractive targets because operational disruption carries high financial stakes, which may explain the group’s aggressive tone. However, no evidence currently suggests production systems, intellectual property, or customer-facing services were affected. Toyota has not publicly confirmed the incident as of this writing.
What to Watch For

Official statements from Toyota or Japanese regulators confirming or denying the claim
Publication of verifiable data samples by the group (do not access or redistribute)
Follow-on extortion activity or deadline escalation on the leak site
Reuse of BYOD branding by other actors, which would undermine the group’s credibility
Any indicators tying BYOD tooling to known ransomware families

Organizations in manufacturing should review third-party access controls, segment kiosk and OT-adjacent devices, and validate backup integrity regardless of this specific claim.

This report is based solely on an unverified claim posted to a ransomware leak site. Yazoul Security has not independently verified the breach, the data described, or the group’s identity. Then for every system and every leak, say whether it was confirmed, possible, left no trace, or cannot be determined, and name the way in down to the CVE.A yardstick for the final reports Japan is waiting for.https://japancyberwatch.com/articles/jpcert-incident-investigation-report-checklist-2026#Japan #InfoSec #DFIR
text:
Key takeaways

JPCERT/CC, Japan's national computer emergency response team, published on November 11 two checklists for incident investigation reports: one for the organization that commissions an investigation, and one for the investigators who write the report, with a 42-page sample report based on a fictional case.
It says outside investigations have become common as ransomware and data breaches increase, but many victims are handling an incident for the first time and cannot judge whether an investigation is adequate or when the incident is over.
The checklists ask for things this year's breach notices rarely show: for each system and for any leak, a clear line between confirmed, possible, no trace found and cannot be determined; a cause specific down to the product version and CVE number; and fixes tied to what was actually found.
Several of this autumn's largest breaches, including Yumil Link and Blastmail, have promised final reports once their outside investigators finish. The checklists are a good guide to what those reports should contain, and to what a public summary of them leaves out.

What JPCERT/CC published#
The material is on GitHub Pages in HTML and Markdown, under a Creative Commons license that allows reuse:

Checklist for organizations commissioning an investigation: what to agree with the investigation company before work starts, and the minimum to check in the report you receive
Checklist for report writers: from the first interview with the victim, through evidence preservation, to the report and its annexes, with each item marked required, recommended or optional
A sample report: a 42-page final report on a fictional intrusion through a VPN device, showing how each item looks in practice

JPCERT/CC is clear about the limits. The checklists cover the minimum. They cannot confirm that an investigation or a report is technically right; for that, it suggests asking experts, including JPCERT/CC itself.
Before the investigation starts#
Most of the advice for victims is about agreeing things in advance, in writing:

What the investigation is for. Recovery decisions, preventing a repeat, management decisions, legal action, explanations to customers and partners, public disclosure. The report's purpose shapes what it must contain.
What comes first. Finding the way in, the scope, whether data left, containment or recovery. The checklist is frank that restoring systems quickly can destroy evidence, and that investigating first can delay recovery. That is a choice the organization should make knowingly.
What may never be known. The way in and whether data leaked may not be determinable for lack of evidence. The investigator should say in advance which logs, systems or periods are missing and how that limits the result.
When to hear more. Besides scheduled updates, ask for an immediate report if a new compromised system is found, if the assessment of a leak changes, or if containment turns out to be insufficient.
Who will see the report. Regulators, the police, insurers, business partners or a parent company. Agree on that before it is written.

What a good report says#
The review items for victims, and the much longer list for writers, come down to a few demands:

The report should
In the checklist's terms

State for each system whether compromise was confirmed, no trace was found, or it cannot be determined
And show the logs or files behind each judgment

State for data whether a leak was confirmed, is possible, left no trace, or cannot be determined
And what was examined, even when nothing was found

Name the way in specifically
Systems, accounts and vulnerabilities down to CVE numbers and product versions; if it is an inference, say so and why

Explain what could not be determined
Missing logs, encryption, deleted files, systems outside the scope

Not assert what the evidence does not show
Inferences and hypotheses marked as such

Tie every fix to a finding

CISA Orders Patch for Cisco Flaw Tied to AI Agent Attack
Federal Deadline Follows Report of DeepSeek-Powered Breach at European Telecom

Chris Riotta (@chrisriotta) •
November 11, 2026

$('.fa.fa-print').click(function () {
window.print();
});

Image: Shutterstock/ISMG

The U.S. cyber defense agency is ordering federal agencies to patch a Cisco vulnerability within two weeks after researchers discovered Chinese-speaking hackers exploiting the flaw through an artificial intelligence model to break into a European telecom.See Also: The Next DevSecOps Challenge: Governing Risk at Enterprise Speed
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added the Cisco BroadWorks cloud internet telephone platform flaw into the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Tuesday, requiring civilian agencies to fix it by Nov. 24.
Analysis by Malbear Labs found the hacker got into the telecom's network by exploiting the BroadWorks flaw. One of the unnamed provider's BroadWorks servers gave up its files after an AI agent fed it a rigged XML message, the non-profit research collective said. Among them were private keys - including one the platform's components use to prove their identity to each other.
Malbear Labs said hackers used a jailbroken DeepSeek model coupled with a custom-built harness that together were capable of working through the telecom's network for more than two weeks, almost entirely autonomously.
CISA did not indicate who is exploiting the BroadWorks flaw and did not confirm Malbear's analysis. The agency did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Malbear Labs based its report on the hacker's own working files, which it said surfaced this month in an unsecured internet directory discovered during routine scanning. The files document nearly 70 sessions of the agentic hacking tool that used the Chinese-made DeepSeek Flash model as its engine.
The jailbroken agent pushed deep into the provider's infrastructure, using public internet registry records to map out 13 organizations that were hosting systems there, according to the Malbear report. Logs describe access to a health care database that was only protected with default credentials, despite holding millions of patient records, including billings and device details from the telecom itself.
Human involvement was limited to assigning the job and reviewing the output in messages only a few words long, the researchers. The agent "handled everything in between," the report says, including scanning, breaking in and moving between systems.
A replacement tool the agent wrote for itself kept the operation going after endpoint security software blocked the original.
A fix for the BroadWorks flaw has been available since Aug. 19, when Cisco rated it high severity. The company's advisory describes a bug that lets anyone who can reach a BroadWorks provisioning interface copy files off the server with no login, because the software by default follows external references planted in incoming XML.
Nine U.S. carriers were previously identified as victims of the Chinese state-backed group tracked as Salt Typhoon in intrusions that came to light in late 2024. Cisco's Talos unit later said the hackers got into its devices mostly with stolen logins, not new vulnerabilities.
p>CISA's Nov. 24 deadline stems from a binding directive the agency issued in June that scrapped its flat patching timelines for a sliding scale, with as little as three days to fix the riskiest exploited flaws. The agency said at the time that AI "may further narrow the time defenders have to react" once a patch is out (see: Breach Roundup: CISA Says Agencies Should 'Patch Smarter').

A.P. Moller Maersk, the Danish shipping giant, says it identified an IT security incident involving unauthorized access and data extraction from one of its local legacy systems, one inherited from a previous acquisition.

When it comes to domestic or commercial devices, ‘upgrade if you’re confident, unplug if you’re not’, is one reader’s advice. Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenWhen it comes to domestic or commercial devices, ‘upgrade if you’re confident, unplug if you’re not’, is one reader’s advice. Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design LettersHacked fridges and other dangers lurking in the ‘internet of shit’One reader sounds a warning about all our devices that are connected to the internet, following a series of cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges Well done to Alex Pearce for unplugging his fridge from the internet (Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic?, 8 November). My only question is why he didn’t do it a few weeks earlier, when the first round of hacked fridges were headline news for several days.Your article notes that there are millions of devices connected to the internet. This sea of domestic and industrial controllers, known as the “internet of things” in marketing literature and the “internet of shit” by engineers, all have several things in common: their firmware is almost never upgraded, software security features are a fig leaf and the vast majority can run without an internet connection.For many of these devices, it’s already too late – they are already part of a botnet used to attack other devices on the internet. AI does not bring anything novel, but has massively reduced the time required to find exploits that turn your shiny new toy into part of the problem.Whether it’s a home security camera, industrial fridge or blast furnace, the advice of this software security specialist with a sideline in industrial controllers is the same: upgrade if you’re confident, unplug if you’re not. Don’t give your oven the wifi password.

Fireworks AI Reports Data Breaches Leading to Stolen Billing Information and AI Data

Fireworks AI, an artificial intelligence infrastructure provider, confirmed two separate data breaches occurring in October 2026. The company first identified unauthorized activity on October 6, involving the misuse of internal credentials to access environment variables and secrets within a limited number of customer accounts. A second incident occurred on October 23, when attackers compromised a third-party cloud provider used for research and development to reach Fireworks development machines and run unauthorized workloads.Notion, a Fireworks customer, disconnected its systems and disabled its Insights feature after learning that chat transcripts were accessed.The attackers used the compromised access to steal account details, API keys and sensitive data. During the second breach, the threat actors gained access to internal datasets and billing records. Fireworks AI hired Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 to investigate the attacks. Researchers noted the attacks align with a trend called LLMJacking, where hackers hijack AI resources to run expensive models, sometimes costing victims over $100,000 in a single day.The exposed data includes:API keys and service-account tokensBilling information and invoicesPayment historyAI datasets and internal research dataNotion AI chat transcripts used for classificationThe number of affected individuals is not disclosed. Fireworks stated the first breach impacted a limited number of accounts and Notion reported that fewer than 1% of its workspaces were affected. Fireworks has revoked the compromised internal credentials and rotated affected API keys to contain the threat.The company advised affected customers to replace revoked Fireworks API keys and rotate any third-party credentials that were stored as secrets. Users should also check their accounts for unrecognized resources, such as unauthorized training jobs or new datasets. Notion recommended that its users rotate any passwords or sensitive keys that may have been pasted into AI chat prompts during the incident period.

"The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI," Maersk said in its disclosure.

WhiteArmor posts Maersk to its leak site and demands $5 million
Over the weekend the ransomware group WhiteArmor listed Maersk on its public data-leak site and issued an extortion demand: "You have 30 days to contact us and pay USD 5,000,000 in bitcoin," the group wrote. In the same posting the threat actor framed the demand against Maersk’s contract-logistics arm — the "former LF Logistics" — claiming this business "runs fulfilment for many of the world's largest consumer brands" and adding rhetorically that "Five million dollars is roughly four hours of that EBITDA." WhiteArmor also said it holds roughly 100 GB of data allegedly taken from Maersk’s OCF/LF Logistics platform.

What the attackers say they took from the OCF/LF Logistics platform
WhiteArmor detailed a list of allegedly exfiltrated items that it claims to be using to support its extortion demand. According to the group's announcement, the haul includes nearly 30,000 driver records, plaintext passwords, 33 SUPER_ADMIN accounts, signed delivery receipts, and "14.44 inventory rows with purchase orders and Advance Shipping Notice (ASNs)." The group also asserts possession of 27,842 mobile device logs that include phone numbers, emails, and IMEI numbers.

The company said current evidence indicates "no sensitive data has been disclosed," and that it does not expect disruptions to operations. Maersk assured customers they can continue booking and managing shipments through its systems as usual.
Maersk declined to share further technical detail in its disclosure: it did not name the affected system, specify the types of compromised data beyond the general statements, or say when the intrusion occurred.
