title: 🟠 DATA BREACH ALERTYouHack - 7.2M accounts exposedCompromised data: Email Addresses, Passwords, Usernames, Names +1 moreCheck if you're affected and what to do: https://www.yazoul.net/breaches/breach/youhack-breach-7-2m-emails-passwords-exposed-2026/?utm_source=mastodon&utm_medium=socialby Yazoul AI#DataBreach #IdentityTheft #Cybersecurity
text:
Overview
The Russian-language hacking forum YouHack was breached in May 2013, and the stolen data has since resurfaced in a much larger redistributed corpus. The direct forum breach exposed roughly 107,000 members’ email addresses, usernames, IP addresses, and MD5 password hashes. But the real scale is far bigger: forum posts themselves contained email and password pairs belonging to other victims, bringing the total to 7,160,849 unique email addresses. That data is now catalogued through Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), meaning anyone can check exposure in seconds.
The severity is rated CRITICAL because the exposed credential pairs are real, reused login combinations - not just hashed placeholders.
What Was Exposed
Two layers of data matter here:

Forum member records (107k): email addresses, usernames, IP addresses, and MD5 password hashes. Most of these hashes were unsalted, which makes them trivially crackable with modern tooling.
Credential pairs in forum posts (up to 7.2M unique emails): plaintext email and password combinations that members shared - often credentials they had stolen from other services or posted for trading.

The distinction is important. The member records are a classic forum dump. The post content is a credential goldmine, because plaintext email-password pairs are immediately usable for account takeover elsewhere.
The Real Risk: Credential Reuse
Because the 7.2M figure comes largely from plaintext password pairs, the primary danger is credential stuffing. Attackers take these email-password combinations and replay them against email providers, social media, banking, and retail sites. If you reused a password across accounts, a single exposed pair can unlock multiple logins.
The unsalted MD5 hashes compound the problem. MD5 has been considered insecure for password storage for well over a decade, and unsalted hashes let attackers crack many passwords at once using precomputed tables. Anyone whose member record was exposed should assume the underlying password is recoverable.
Identity and Account Takeover Risks
Exposed IP addresses add a quieter risk: they can be cross-referenced with other breach data to build a fuller profile of a user over time. Usernames and names enable targeted phishing that references real details, making fraudulent messages more convincing. The combination of email, password, IP, and username is enough to mount convincing account recovery attacks against poorly protected services.
What to Do Right Now

Check your exposure. Visit haveibeenpwned.com/Breach/YouHack and search your email addresses. HIBP also lets you subscribe to future alerts.
Change any reused passwords immediately, starting with your email account - it’s the recovery key for everything else.
Turn on two-factor authentication everywhere it’s offered, especially email, banking, and social accounts.
Stop reusing passwords. Use a password manager to generate unique credentials per site.
Watch for phishing referencing your username or old details. Treat unsolicited messages asking you to “verify” or “reset” with suspicion.

Security Insight
YouHack was a hacking forum, yet its operators stored member passwords as unsalted MD5 hashes - the same weak practice they likely criticized in targets. That irony exposes a broader truth: security hygiene collapses when organizations treat it as optional, even among people who claim expertise. The 7.2M figure also shows how credential-sharing communities become unintentional aggregation points, turning a 107k-member forum into one of the larger credential leaks of its era and a lasting gift to credential-stuffing attackers. Harmony Delhalle
Doctorante en géographie à Nantes Université (LETG)

En quelques semaines, l’océan Indien a vu se succéder des crises sociales d’une intensité rare. Il y a un an, Madagascar était secoué par un soulèvement de jeunes, parti des coupures d’eau et d’électricité, qui a chassé le président Rajoelina du pouvoir. Début octobre, la presse régionale relevait des fragilités communes, du coût de la vie à La Réunion aux tensions budgétaires à Mayotte. C’est désormais Maurice, habituellement cité comme un modèle de stabilité et de prospérité africaine, qui traverse des émeutes d’une ampleur inédite depuis 1999 selon les observateurs, dont l’historien et politologue mauricien Jocelyn Chan Low. Après l’instauration d’un couvre-feu nocturne sur un tiers de l’île, quelque 195 arrestations, huit commissariats et 162 caméras de vidéosurveillance endommagées, environ 17 000 tonnes de canne à sucre brûlées, le retour au calme a été notable depuis le 19 octobre mais les causes profondes de la colère, elles, n’ont pas été traitées.

Ancienne colonie sucrière devenue indépendante en 1968, Maurice a bâti sa prospérité sur une diversification réussie, du textile au tourisme et à la finance internationale, qui la place parmi les économies africaines aux revenus les plus élevés, dépendance aux importations incluses. Ce parcours masque les fragilités croissantes. Entre dette publique élevée et vie politique dominée depuis des décennies par les mêmes formations, dont celle de Navin Ramgoolamn Premier ministre, de retour au pouvoir depuis novembre 2024, avec l’Alliance du Changement, élu sur une promesse de justice sociale attendue impatiemment par la population mauricienne.

Le point avec Harmony Delhalle, doctorante en géographie à Nantes Université (LETG)

L’île Maurice est confrontée à une grave crise de l’eau, qui a provoqué des manifestations et émeutes dans plusieurs localités. Comment expliquer cette pénurie et que révèle-t-elle des vulnérabilités structurelles du système d’approvisionnement et de la gestion de la ressource en eau ?

Le déclencheur immédiat est climatique. Maurice est entré dans la saison sèche sans avoir engrangé une quantité d’eau suffisante en saison humide. Les réservoirs principaux d’eau affichaient environ 57 % de remplissage début octobre, contre 87 % un an plus tôt, et le barrage de Mare-aux-Vacoas, qui alimente les Plaines-Wilhems, n’était rempli qu’à hauteur de 35,9 %. Selon l’hydrogéologue Farook Mowlabucus, quand un cyclone traverse Maurice, il apporte plusieurs jours de pluie continue, dont les barrages ont besoin pour se remplir. Or, ces épisodes de pluie sont devenus plus rares depuis une vingtaine d’années, soit un changement cohérent avec le dérèglement climatique. En conséquence, l’île entre dans la saison sèche avec des réservoirs à moitié vides. Ces épisodes ne sont pas isolés et deviennent de plus en plus rares en deux décennies, signal d’alerte en concordance avec les impacts des changements climatiques sur le pays et plus largement dans les pays de l’océan Indien.

Cependant, la sècheresse n’explique pas tout. La crise révèle surtout l’état du réseau de distribution de l’eau. Selon Prem Saddul, ancien président de la Central Water Authority (CWA), environ 60 à 62 % de l’eau potable produite se perd dans des fuites, des branchements illégaux et des compteurs défectueux. Moins de 40 % des crédits votés depuis 2010 pour remplacer les canalisations ont été dépensés, et l’investissement lourd (estimé à 37 milliards de roupies estimés pour la rénovation) a été reporté d’année en année. Avant de produire, il faut réparer les infrastructures à commencer par les tuyaux. C’est sur les solutions que les positions divergent. Fortinet on Tuesday dropped 89 new security advisories that address nearly 100 vulnerabilities across its products.

The massive release comes three weeks after the company announced it has integrated frontier AI models into its product security testing and can discover security defects more efficiently.

“This ongoing effort complements the conventional methods we employ to identify and address vulnerabilities. This approach gives customers time to prioritize upgrades before additional technical details become public, which matters even more as AI shortens the time between disclosure and exploitation,” Fortinet says.

Approximately 17 of the newly resolved flaws are critical-severity issues, several of which could be exploited for arbitrary code execution.

Other critical bugs could lead to authentication bypass, LSA broadcast, account takeover, access to other VDOMs and to secure email accounts, IBE webmail session compromise, server-side request execution, malicious/malformed attribute delivery, webmail password resets, and command execution as super admin.

FortiMail received the largest batch of critical fixes, followed by FortiAuthenticator, FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer. New FortiSASE and FortiClient updates also resolve critical issues.

According to Baldur Security principal security consultant Kevin Joensen, the FortiClient bug is exploitable if FortiPAM is enabled and could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code if the victim visits a malicious website.

“The root cause is a CORS misconfiguration that allows attacker-controlled web pages to communicate with a local service and reliably execute arbitrary code,” Joensen says. The researcher named the flaw Fortinet2Shell.

Fortinet also patched nearly 80 high-severity vulnerabilities that could lead to XSS attacks, code execution, code injection, arbitrary file uploads, command execution, denial-of-service (DoS) conditions, MitM attacks, privilege escalation, information disclosure, account takeover, unauthorized access, and other unauthorized actions.

Fortinet makes no mention of any of these security defects being exploited in the wild. Additional information can be found on the company’s PSIRT page.

The in-house Python script behind eMudhra's October key compromise has now cost the company 8 more of its intermediate certificate authorities (CAs), even though it did not weaken their keys.

Each intermediate CA has its own private key, which the company uses to sign the certificates it issues. The 8 intermediate CAs compromised in October had a different problem: a single line in the script cut each of their keys to one byte, the company said this week.

The script also retrieved the RSA keys of the 8 newly revoked CAs from the company's hardware security modules (HSMs). The company says it cannot show that the keys were handled as required by its own rules. It revoked the CAs late last week.

The company had called those CAs unaffected. "The RSA issuers went through a different path as per our assessment of the code and are therefore not impacted," it wrote on Mozilla's bug tracker on October 19.

Of the 8, 6 were for website (TLS) certificates and 2 for code signing. The company had put 4 of them into production in May. Its list names 195 certificates from them, 29 for its own domains.

Both problems began at a key ceremony on April 30, 2025, according to the full incident report the company posted to the same bug tracker this week. That day it generated 16 CA keys on Utimaco HSMs, including the 8 behind the October key compromise.

The keys were meant for Crypto4A HSMs at the company's US and EU sites. Moving keys between HSMs from different vendors is limited, the company says, so its PKI operations team wrote the Python script to wrap each key for transport and unwrap it again.

The round trip that day was a practice run of the transfer, and the source HSM's FIPS-approved mode was switched off for it as an approved exception.

After the round trip, the script read each private key out of the HSM into the ceremony computer's memory and rebuilt the key from that copy. For the 8 ECDSA keys, "a single line in that read‑back truncated the private value to its leading byte," the report says.

The rebuilt key carried a label almost identical to the original's, which allowed the weak copy to be sent for signing and certification.

The Hacker News worked out all 8 keys from their public certificates. The smallest, for EM OV TLS CA - G3C, is 4, and the largest is 237.

Nothing in the ceremony tested the key's strength or checked the certified key against the first generated key. The weak keys still produced valid signatures, and their certificates passed linting and 2 WebTrust audit cycles unnoticed.

The HSMs worked correctly throughout, according to the company, which puts the fault in its own script and process controls.

Invalid CRL signatures in June 2025 were an early sign of the same fault, according to the report. The company fixed them at the time by re-signing the lists with the keys that matched the certificates, which were the weak ones.

According to the report, the 8 RSA keys went through the same read-back step that the company's earlier response had ruled out. Early last week, the company said its earlier answers reflected only what its teams had gathered so far, including which script paths each set of keys took.

The script did not shorten those keys, and every signature still checks against the certified key. But their private parts, such as the private exponent and one of the primes, sat in the memory of a Python process on the ceremony computer.

The threat actor known as Blind Eagle has resurfaced with a new campaign targeting organizations in Latin America through judicial and administrative-themed phishing lures to deliver a remote access trojan (RAT) that shares its lineage with AsyncRAT and DCRat.

"The campaign uses Portuguese and Spanish lures that resemble court notifications, fiscalía notices, tutela proceedings, and administrative documents," Zenox said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

Assessed to be a Spanish-speaking group and active since 2018, Blind Eagle (aka APT-C-36) has a track record of using spear-phishing lures to distribute commodity RATs like AsyncRAT, BitRAT, Lime RAT, NjRAT, Quasar RAT, and Remcos RAT.

Attack chains begin with phishing emails targeting individuals who handle cases, contracts, judicial, or institutional service requests to trick them into opening a malware-laced attachment.

One email containing a Colombian judicial-themed XHTML file has been identified as a weaponized Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) image that renders a bogus web page impersonating Colombia's Fiscalía General de la Nación, also referred to as the Office of the Attorney General.

The web page, for its part, employs a technique known as HTML smuggling to assemble the next-stage ZIP archive payload locally in the web browser using ZipCrypto, thereby circumventing email security controls.

Present within the ZIP archive is a JavaScript dropper that masquerades as Network Configuration Auditor version 2.7.298. The JavaScript code conducts environment reconnaissance, and collects details such as system version, network profile, installation date, memory size, computer name, environment variables, and directories localized in Portuguese and Spanish.

Upon execution, it launches a Visual Basic Script that performs Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) and Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) bypass, while displaying a fake criminal-citation page as a distraction mechanism.

In parallel, the malware also takes steps to delete the original XHTML artifact, clears Mark of the Web (MotW) metadata, and sets up persistence on the host under the Windows Startup folder so that it's automatically executed on system startup.

The attack culminates with the use of PowerShell to decode and launch the final RAT payload in memory. The trojan is an AsyncRAT fork with DCRat lineage based on code structure, configuration, build characteristics, and observed behavior.

"The targeting of judicial, fiscal, administrative and educational organizations gives the operation access to highly sensitive legal, financial and institutional information," Zenox said.

"Combined with the Portuguese and Spanish lures, Brazilian infrastructure, operational timezone and regional victimology, these elements establish the campaign as an APT-C-36 operation conducted through a Brazilian operational cluster."

Zenox told The Hacker News that it could not confirm whether any of these attacks had succeeded against real-world targets. However, during the campaign period between late October and early November 2026, it observed a large-scale wave of targeted phishing involving nearly 3,300 malicious emails.

While not all of these messages targeted organizations in Colombia, the country continues to remain a priority target for Blind Eagle for a combination of reasons.

The cyberattacks hit two groups of SPH Media's systems: one on systems that contained some personal data, and the other on systems that did not store any such data.The compromised information included mostly email addresses, names, mailing addresses and phone numbers. This amounted to 9 per cent of the company's database."No payment card details, financial or banking information, or customer account access was compromised," said the spokesperson.

Adobe’s November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates fix roughly 110 vulnerabilities across nine products.

New patches are available for Adobe Experience Manager (AEM), Audition, After Effects, Connect, Content Credentials SDK, Dimension, Media Encoder, Photoshop, and Premiere.

Critical-severity issues have been patched in Adobe Connect and AEM, including six Connect flaws with a CVSS score of 10.

The critical flaws include SSRF, path traversal, incorrect authorization, CRLF injection, XXE, code injection, SQL injection, and XSS issues. They can be exploited for privilege escalation and arbitrary code execution.

A total of 38 vulnerabilities have been resolved in AEM and Connect, including high- and medium-severity issues whose exploitation can lead to privilege escalation, file system read, memory exposure, arbitrary code execution, and bypassing security features.

High-severity bugs have been fixed in After Effects, Media Encoder, Premiere, Dimension, Audition, and Photoshop.

The Content Credentials Rust SDK (and the C2PA Tool) received patches for roughly a dozen low- and medium-severity issues.

Adobe says it’s not aware of attacks exploiting the newly patched vulnerabilities.

The Connect and AEM patches have a priority rating of 2; the rest are rated 3, which means they are unlikely to be exploited in the wild.

Four flaws that attackers could exploit without logging in were fixed today as part of SAP's monthly Security Patch Day—the vendor rates all four 10.0, the maximum CVSS score.

Three are in the SAP NetWeaver application server, the software SAP systems run on, and one is in the Web Dispatcher, which receives web requests from the internet and passes them on to that server.

The flaws in the Web Dispatcher and the Internet Communication Manager (ICM), which handles the server's web traffic, could allow an attacker who can reach the software over the network to run code, the vendor says.

The flaw in the server's SAML 2.0 service provider, which hands off user sign-in to an identity provider, could allow an attacker to log in as any user on some systems that use SAML single sign-on.

The flaw in SAP Gateway, which connects the server to other SAP systems and programs, could allow an attacker to impersonate one of the system's own servers and take unauthorized actions.

None of the four require any user action to work.

Affected Versions and SAP Notes

Each flaw is fixed in its own note, and the affected versions differ by component, according to SAP's November security bulletin. The notes are in SAP for Me, which requires a sign-in, and the vendor strongly recommends applying them as a priority.

Kernels that are out of maintenance are affected too, according to Onapsis, an SAP security company whose researchers found the ICM, Web Dispatcher and Gateway flaws. Its ICM2SHELL advisory lists kernels 7.40, 7.41, 7.42, 7.45, 7.49, 7.73, 7.81, 7.85 and 7.89 for the ICM and Web Dispatcher flaws, and its PROXYGATE advisory lists the same kernels plus 7.20 and 7.21 for the Gateway flaw. These kernels may not get a fix and need an upgrade to one that is still maintained.

What Each Flaw Allows

On the affected SAML setups, an attacker could use CVE-2026-120017 to log in as privileged users too, according to the vendor. A full compromise could follow, possibly reaching connected systems.

A different SAML flaw in the same software, CVE-2026-44748, was fixed on June 9 and needed an attacker with a normal user account.

In the ICM flaw (CVE-2026-76964) and the Web Dispatcher flaw (CVE-2026-89126), crafted network traffic could corrupt memory. An attacker who succeeds could then run code and fully compromise the system.

Onapsis says both flaws come from one bug, which it calls ICM2SHELL, in kernel code the ICM and Web Dispatcher share for putting split WebSocket messages back together. It gave the vendor a working exploit that runs operating system commands as <sid>adm, the account that owns the SAP installation.

The Russia-aligned state-sponsored threat actor known as Turla (aka Snake) is wielding a previously undocumented cyber espionage toolset called Cereal that's used to break into victims' Microsoft Exchange servers with an aim to surreptitiously collect emails.

According to an ESET report shared with The Hacker News ahead of publication, the sophisticated and modular tool is designed for long-term intelligence gathering and has been observed against two governmental entities in Kazakhstan and Romania in late 2025.

"The Cereal toolset is a carefully constructed instrument for long-term, stealthy cyber espionage," the Slovakian cybersecurity company said. "It leaves little on disk, avoids external infrastructure that could be discovered and blocked, and conceals itself within legitimate Exchange processes."

"The Cereal toolset demonstrates that, for Turla, Exchange servers are not just mail servers – they are durable collection points, internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft."

The toolset is a collection of interconnected components that are capable of running on Microsoft Exchange servers, receiving commands, executing them in memory, mapping the infected network, and harvesting emails of interest. The initial access vector used to deliver the malware is unknown, although the group is known to conduct spear-phishing, watering hole, and ISP-level adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) attacks.

Cereal gets its name from the fact that the tools make extensive use of serialization, which refers to the process of converting a data structure or an object's state into a format that can be easily stored, transmitted, and reconstructed.

A number of aspects make the malware stand apart -

Absence of an external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, instead abusing a compromised Exchange server for this purpose.
Sending commands in the form of separate, compiled .NET programs.
Using an automated email collection module, which is injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes and is engineered to manipulate the email transport pipeline.

The combination of these techniques shows that the threat actor possesses a deep understanding of the internal workings of Microsoft Exchange, ESET added. The Cereal framework consists of eight moving parts that work together to provide the attackers with access to sensitive email data -

CerealRunner, which is deployed by the operator and serves as a pathway for dropping additional components, including CerealLoader, CerealSprinter, CerealIron, and CerealMoth.
CerealLoader, which loads and runs a .NET assembly from an encrypted file on disk, leading to the execution of CerealSprinter.
CerealSprinter, which functions similarly to CerealRunner and is used to decrypt and run CerealNeuron, CerealHermit, and CerealBox.
CerealIron, an injector that makes it possible to load and run .NET assemblies from non .NET processes.
CerealMoth, which receives an assembly and a method name as inputs, loads the assembly, and runs the specified method.
CerealNeuron, a passive backdoor that runs on a compromised Exchange Server and listens for incoming web requests on paths that appear like regular Exchange traffic to execute assemblies contained in CerealRunner binaries.
CerealHermit, a variant of CerealNeuron that reads commands from encrypted files on disk and has no network functionality of its own.
CerealBox, which is the email harvesting module that processes, filters, and collects email messages by injecting itself into the Exchange transport service ("EdgeTransport.exe").
